name: Marco Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hillcrest Dairy, three hundred cows milked twice a day in a parlour, the shed where the cows come in and stand in rows to be milked. I do the early milking, starting at half four, then wash down, feed the calves and help Andrew, the owner, with whatever the cows need. By eleven I've done a day's work, and I'm back at three for the afternoon milking.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You came to dairy late, I think?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drove lorries for thirty-two years, long distance, all over. My back and my marriage both told me to stop, so at fifty-five I did. My grandfather had a little farm with twelve cows, and I'd always wanted to try, so I knocked on Andrew's door and said I'd do any shift he hated.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the cows' routine. They walk into the parlour in nearly the same order every morning, like people taking their seats in church. What wears me out is the early starts in winter, and how much I still don't know. Andrew can watch a cow walk across the yard and tell you her foot's sore, and I'm still checking my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great tool and everyone should try it. I use it every day. Each cow wears a collar that tracks how much she chews and walks, and I ask an AI to help me read the numbers and spot the ones that might be sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the thing that makes up for my lack of experience. Andrew knows by looking, and I know by asking the phone, and between us we catch most things. It's not as good as thirty years, but it's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, but more. I'd learn the collar software properly, and maybe show Andrew a few tricks, because he only uses it for heat, for knowing when a cow is ready to breed. Teresa, my wife, and I would keep about four months saved, and I'd keep putting a little in the church collection, as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, happy even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about a time the phone caught something.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In March a cow, number 212, had normal milk but her chewing had dropped by a third overnight. I asked the AI what that might mean, and it said check for a stomach problem. The vet came, and it was a twisted stomach, caught early, and she's still in the herd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Andrew mind you showing him tricks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, he's proud. So I do it like I'm asking him, not telling him. Andrew, does this look right to you? And he says, yes, obviously, and then he uses it.

S0.say: I'd say it's a great tool and everyone should try it. I use it every day to read the cows' collar data and spot ones that might be sick.
S0.think: Privately it makes up for my lack of experience. Andrew knows by looking and I know by asking the phone, and between us we catch most things.
S0.do: Learns the collar software properly and quietly shows Andrew new tricks. Keeps about four months of savings with his wife Teresa and keeps giving to the church collection.
S0.quote: Andrew knows by looking, and I know by asking the phone, and between us we catch most things.
S0.fieldNote: Marco treats AI as a crutch for his inexperience and isn't embarrassed about it. The story of cow 212 shows real value, not just enthusiasm. He's tactful with his proud boss, which suggests he's thought about how change lands on people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow change is good, it gives families time. Farms not hiring beginners is a problem, so we need proper apprenticeships, a young person learning beside an old hand. That's how my grandfather taught my father.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm fine. I'm the old beginner who brings the tech, so I'm cheap and useful. But my grandson Luca, he's seventeen and wants to work with cows, and he's the one who'd be shut out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Andrew to take Luca on two days a week as an apprentice, and I'd train him myself. I'd look for any grant for small farms taking apprentices. And I'd keep learning the software, maybe a short course on cow health online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of worry for Luca.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's Luca like with the cows?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than me already, honestly. He walks in slow, talks to them, and they don't move away from him. He's got what Andrew's got, and I just have the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Andrew take him on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I promise Luca will turn up at half four, yes. The farmers round here have all had young ones who didn't last a winter. I'd tell Andrew, if he's late once, I'll do his shift and he'll never hear the end of it from his grandmother.

S1.say: I'd say slow change gives families time, and since farms aren't hiring beginners we need proper apprenticeships beside an old hand.
S1.think: Off the record I'm fine, because I'm a cheap, useful old beginner who brings the tech. But my seventeen-year-old grandson Luca, who wants to work with cows, could be shut out.
S1.do: Asks Andrew to take Luca on two days a week as an apprentice and trains him himself. Looks for grants for small farms taking apprentices and takes a short online cow health course.
S1.feel: Calm, with a little worry for his grandson.
S1.quote: He's got what Andrew's got, and I just have the phone.
S1.fieldNote: His traditional values show up as an apprenticeship plan, built around a real grandson. He's honest that Luca has the instinct he lacks. He's calm about himself because he sees his tech skill as his ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the third. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's hard for office workers, but that's how it goes, things change. People need to get up and learn something new, like I did at fifty-five. The government should help with training and keep out of the way otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's not my world. People still drink milk whether their office has robots or not. My daughter's a teacher and my son's a builder, so my family's mostly safe, thank God.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show anyone who asked how I use these AI assistants, especially people at church who might be worried. I'd maybe offer to help Andrew's wife, Claire, with the farm paperwork using the AI, so she has more time. And I'd keep saving as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit sorry for people, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people need to get up and learn something new. Is it really that simple?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I suppose not. I had a lorry pension and a wife with a job, and I still nearly didn't do it. Some people have nothing behind them, and it's easy for me to sit here and say get up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at church would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bernadette, she's sixty and does the parish accounts and works at an insurance office in town. She already asked me after Mass what these AI things are. I'd sit with her at the coffee morning and show her, slowly.

S2.say: I'd say it's hard for office workers but people need to get up and learn something new, like I did at fifty-five. The government should help with training and otherwise keep out of the way.
S2.think: Privately it's not my world, because people still drink milk. My daughter's a teacher and my son's a builder, so my family is mostly safe.
S2.do: Shows worried church members how he uses AI assistants and offers to help Andrew's wife Claire with farm paperwork. Keeps saving as usual.
S2.feel: Calm, though a bit sorry for people.
S2.quote: Some people have nothing behind them, and it's easy for me to sit here and say get up.
S2.fieldNote: His first answer was the classic self-reliance line, but he softened it himself when challenged. His instinct is to help one person at a time, like Bernadette at the coffee morning. His own family is mostly outside the office world, which keeps him calm here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The fourth one is faster. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who did well should give back to their towns and families, and pay their fair share, not dodge it. But I don't want the government taking over everything either. I'd say it after Mass over coffee, where these arguments always happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd worry about the milk price. If shops and dairies are run by AI, they'll squeeze farmers harder, and Andrew's margins are thin already. And if land prices boom, Andrew's brother might push him to sell, because the family owns the land together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help Andrew cut costs with the collar data, fewer vet bills, fewer cows lost. I'd ask him straight about the brother, man to man. And Teresa and I would put a bit extra away, maybe an extra fifty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Physical jobs safe, they say, but the farm runs on a milk price someone else sets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Andrew man to man. What would he say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say, Marco, don't worry about it, which is what he always says when he's worried. Then two days later he'd tell me more. He's like a cow that way, you have to let him come to you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a house now, if prices were booming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we've got our little house and it's enough. I'd tell my son not to buy at the top either, but he wouldn't listen. Builders always think prices only go up.

S3.say: I'd say the people who did well should give back to their towns and pay their fair share, but I don't want the government taking over everything. I'd say it over coffee after Mass.
S3.think: I'd worry that AI-run dairies and shops squeeze the milk price. If land prices boom, Andrew's brother might push him to sell the family land.
S3.do: Helps Andrew cut costs using the collar data and asks him directly about his brother. Puts away about fifty a week extra with Teresa.
S3.feel: Uneasy, because the farm depends on a milk price someone else sets.
S3.quote: He's like a cow that way, you have to let him come to you.
S3.fieldNote: He looks past the 'physical jobs are safe' line to the milk price and the family land. His traditional view still wants a fair share paid, just not a government takeover. He reads his boss the same patient way he reads cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. This is the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms aren't new, milking robots have been around for years. The question is whether we use them well and keep families on the land. I'd say farms should get help to train their own people, not bring in companies from outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, Andrew has been pricing two milking robots since last year. If general robots come on top, for feeding, scraping and calves, my early shift is gone. My grandfather milked twelve cows by hand. I milk three hundred with a machine. My grandson might milk none and still be called a dairyman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Andrew in the first month and say, let me be the robot man. I already read the collar data, so I'd learn the robot software, the alarms, the cleaning, all of it, and do the maker's course. And I'd make sure Luca learned it beside me, so there's a young one ready when I retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and excited. I'm not scared of the machine, I'm scared of being too old for them to bother training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Andrew says he'd rather hire a young technician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to the next farm that buys one, and there will be plenty. I've changed my whole life once at fifty-five, I can change farms at sixty. Teresa would say I'm stubborn, and she'd be right, but stubborn in a useful direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the cows miss the people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would, the old ones, the ones that like their necks scratched. The young ones would never know any different. That's the sad part, maybe, not for the cows but for us.

S4.say: I'd say robots on farms aren't new, and the question is whether we use them well and keep families on the land. Farms should get help to train their own people.
S4.think: I think if general robots arrive on top of the milking robots Andrew has been pricing, my early shift is gone. My grandson might milk none and still be called a dairyman.
S4.do: Asks Andrew in the first month to make him the robot man and takes the maker's course on the software, alarms and cleaning. Brings his grandson Luca along to learn beside him.
S4.feel: Anxious and excited, not scared of the machine but of being too old to be worth training.
S4.quote: My grandfather milked twelve cows by hand. I milk three hundred with a machine. My grandson might milk none and still be called a dairyman.
S4.fieldNote: Marco sees robots as the next step in a family line, not a break in it. His real fear is ageism, not technology. His backup plan is confident because he has already changed his whole life once, and he wants Luca trained alongside him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, the robots, because it's my shift on the line. What would help is help for small family farms to train their own people on the new machines, older ones and young ones together. And a fair milk price, so farmers like Andrew can afford to keep people on at all.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. People will need something to hold on to when work changes this fast. For me it's my family and the church, and the cows, if I'm honest, in that order most days.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Thank you. Now I need to sleep, half four comes quickly.

headlineQuote: My grandfather milked twelve cows by hand. I milk three hundred with a machine. My grandson might milk none and still be called a dairyman.
portrait: Marco is a 58-year-old former long-distance lorry driver who now does the early milking on a 300-cow dairy farm. He uses AI every day to read the cows' collar data, which he admits makes up for his lack of experience. He's traditional, churchgoing and believes in self-reliance and apprenticeships, though he softens when challenged. His worries move from the milk price to the family land, and with robots he plans to become the farm's robot man and train his grandson beside him.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries him most, because it puts his early milking shift on the line and he fears being too old to be worth training.
whatWouldHelp: Help for small family farms to train their own people, young and old together, on new machines, and a fair milk price so farmers can keep staff.
